subject: physics
qualificationNote: Eduqas A level Physics (A420QS)|Linear A level, 3 written components plus a separately reported Practical Endorsement: Component 1 Newtonian Physics (2h15, 100 marks, 31.25%), Component 2 Electricity and the Universe (2h, 100 marks, 31.25%), Component 3 Light, Nuclei and Options (2h15, 120 marks, 37.5%, Section B is 1 option chosen from 4); the AS (B420QS) is a separate qualification whose content is a subset of these components, and the A level document itself prints no AS/A2 labels.

the features of electric and gravitational fields as specified in the table on page 30

ELECTRIC FIELDS: Electric field strength, E, is the force per unit charge on a small positive test charge placed at the point | GRAVITATIONAL FIELDS: Gravitational field strength, g, is the force per unit mass on a small test mass placed at the point

ELECTRIC FIELDS: Inverse square law for the force between two electric charges in the form F = (1/4πε₀)(Q₁Q₂/r²) (Coulomb's law) | GRAVITATIONAL FIELDS: Inverse square law for the force between two masses in the form F = G M₁M₂/r² (Newton's law of gravitation)
ELECTRIC FIELDS: F can be attractive or repulsive | GRAVITATIONAL FIELDS: F is attractive only
ELECTRIC FIELDS: E = (1/4πε₀)(Q/r²) for the field strength due to a point charge in free space or air | GRAVITATIONAL FIELDS: g = GM/r² for the field strength due to a point mass

ELECTRIC FIELDS: Potential at a point due to a point charge in terms of the work done in bringing a unit positive charge from infinity to that point | GRAVITATIONAL FIELDS: Potential at a point due to a point mass in terms of the work done in bringing a unit mass from infinity to that point
ELECTRIC FIELDS: V_E = (1/4πε₀)(Q/r) and PE = (1/4πε₀)(Q₁Q₂/r) | GRAVITATIONAL FIELDS: V_g = −GM/r and PE = −GM₁M₂/r

ELECTRIC FIELDS: Change in potential energy of a point charge moving in any electric field = qΔV_E | GRAVITATIONAL FIELDS: Change in potential energy of a point mass moving in any gravitational field = mΔV_g

ELECTRIC FIELDS: Field strength at a point is given by E = - slope of the V_E – r graph at that point | GRAVITATIONAL FIELDS: Field strength at a point is given by g = - slope of the V_g – r graph at that point
ELECTRIC FIELDS: Note that 1/4πε₀ ≈ 9 x 10⁹ F⁻¹m is an acceptable approximation

how to use equations to determine the moment of inertia, I, for example • a solid sphere I = (2/5)mr² • a thin spherical shell I = (2/3)mr² where m is the mass and r is the radius
the idea that angular acceleration, α, is defined as the rate of change of angular velocity, ω, and how to use the equation α = (ω₂ − ω₁)/t
the idea that torque, τ, is given as τ = Iα
angular momentum, L, is given as L = Iω where ω is the angular velocity
the principle of conservation of angular momentum and use it to solve problems in sporting contexts
how to use the equation for the rotational kinetic energy, rotational KE = ½Iω²
how to use the principle of conservation of energy including the use of linear and rotational kinetic energy as well as gravitational and elastic potential energy in various sporting contexts
how to use projectile motion theory in sporting contexts
how to use Bernoulli's equation p = p₀ − ½ρv² in sporting contexts
how to determine the magnitude of the drag force using F_D = ½ρv²AC_D where C_D is the drag coefficient
how the following affect the rate at which the temperature of the Earth rises including:

the need for thermal equilibrium: that is the balance between energy inflow from the Sun and energy re-radiated from the Earth in the context of global energy demand and the effect of CO₂ levels in the atmosphere
the origin and means of transmission of solar energy and the form of the Sun's power spectrum including the idea that wavelengths are converted into the near infrared in the atmosphere
the use of Wien's law (λ_max T = constant) and Stefan-Boltzman T⁴ law in the context of solar power
use of the density equation and Archimedes' principle to explain why rising sea levels are due to melting ice caps and that the melting of ice on land increases sea levels but melting icebergs do not
the common sources of renewable and non-renewable energy and be able to compare their development and use both in the UK and internationally

wind power: • the power available from a flowing fluid P = ½Aρv³ • the factors affecting the efficiency of wind turbines

the principles of fuel cell operation and the benefits of fuel cells particularly regarding greenhouse gas emissions
the thermal conduction equation in the form ΔQ/Δt = −AK(Δθ/Δx)

the effect of insulation on thermal energy loss and be able to calculate the heat loss for parallel surfaces using the rate of energy transfer = UAΔθ including cases where different materials are in contact
